topic: Why your recorded voice sounds strange: bone conduction, stapedius reflex, self-voice bias
hook: Why your voice sounds weird on recordings
caption:
That cringe when you hear yourself on a voice note is real, and it has a physical cause. In your head, your voice also travels through your skull bones, which boost the low tones. A microphone only picks up the air, so the recording sounds higher and thinner than the voice you know.

The twist: in a 2013 study, people rated their own voice as more attractive when they didn't realize it was theirs. So the problem is mostly surprise.

Be honest: do you still hate hearing your own voice on recordings?

1/5 Two paths to your ear (2)
When you speak, sound reaches your inner ear through the air and through the bones of your skull.
📷 unknown (CC BY 4.0) via wikimedia

2/5 Bones add the bass (Deeper)
Your skull carries low tones well, so in your head your voice sounds deeper and fuller than it really is.
🎨 AI-generated image

3/5 Microphones skip the bones
A recording only captures sound through the air. That thinner, higher voice is what everyone else hears.
📷 Galak76 (CC BY-SA 3.0) via wikimedia

4/5 Your ears turn it down
A tiny middle-ear muscle tightens as you speak, muffling your own voice so it doesn't deafen you.
📷 RWhitwam (CC BY-SA 4.0) via wikimedia

5/5 You actually like it (2013)
